A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FIM research and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. Earlier Appendices A–G correspond to later Appendices B–H; v3 adds Appendices A and I.

before.justification: v2 reports original FIM experiments on dynamical-system reconstruction and time-series imputation, including benchmark results and appendix ablations.

after.justification: v3 retains those original empirical results and adds Lorenz-system fine-tuning experiments in Appendix I and Table 25.

M1.justification: Appendix I adds reconstruction-based fine-tuning of FIM-ell using noisy observations or clean reconstruction targets, without requiring ground-truth derivatives. The core zero-shot architecture, synthetic pretraining framework and inference procedures remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The training and evaluation domains and tasks are retained. Appendix I reuses the existing Lorenz-system data; its fine-tuning procedures do not introduce different dataset or task coverage. Newly discussed meta-learning applications are cited examples, not additional experiments.

E2.justification: The established benchmark comparator rosters remain unchanged. Table 25 adds a limited within-FIM comparison between pretrained, noisy-target fine-tuned and clean-target fine-tuned models. The meta-learning methods newly discussed in Appendix A are not empirically evaluated.

E3.justification: Appendix I introduces a two-epoch fine-tuning protocol with learning rate 1e-6, four training windows and all Lorenz coordinates. It compares noisy and clean reconstruction targets and evaluates multiple window counts. Existing benchmark protocols are retained.

E4.justification: Appendix I adds a controlled study of fine-tuning, sensitivity to noisy reconstruction targets and performance across temporal scales. It also reports qualitative deterioration with longer training or larger learning rates. Earlier architecture, synthetic-data and windowing ablations remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Existing uncertainty practices remain unchanged, including ten corruption samplings for ODEBench and variability across Lorenz trajectories. Table 25 adds results with plus/minus values but introduces no specified new seed count, repeated-run design, significance test or uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Tables 1–24 and existing result figures retain their results. New Table 25 reports, at four windows, 7.136 ± 0.697 for pretrained FIM versus 5.936 ± 0.432 and 5.947 ± 0.433 after noisy-target and clean-target fine-tuning. Effects vary: at twenty windows, the reported error rises from 1.526 to 1.586 and 1.588.

T1.justification: The minimized losses in v2 Appendices B.3/C.3, now C.3/D.3, change the Gaussian negative-log-likelihood terms from negative to positive contributions. This corrects their inconsistency with the retained likelihood-maximization objectives; it does not establish that training implementations changed or experiments were rerun.

C1.justification: The introduction narrows contribution (ii) by removing the assertion that FIM outperforms target-trained state-of-the-art models on the 63 ODE series. The central claims of zero-shot reconstruction and imputation across diverse, high-dimensional datasets remain.

C2.justification: Appendix I adds interpretations concerning fine-tuning feasibility, cross-scale retention and noise robustness, alongside a warning about fitting noise and motivation for a future emission model. Section 4.1 also softens the attribution of rapid Rössler acceleration changes to being outside the training distribution from definite to likely.

D1.justification: v3 supplies a public access link and states that pretrained models, the repository and tutorials are available, replacing the earlier release promise and supplementary-access description. Appendix C.5 newly specifies architectures for existing size and encoder ablations; Appendix I documents fine-tuning hyperparameters.

R1.justification: New Appendix A substantially expands positioning against Neural Statistician, Neural Processes and dynamical meta-learning, distinguishing training domains, transfer assumptions and latent-variable sharing. Section 2 removes historical parameter-estimation, gradient-matching and symbolic-regression discussion, while the introduction adds related FIM work on Markov jump processes and stochastic differential equations.

P1.justification: v3 makes localized prose and terminology edits, shortens related work, promotes the windowing explanation to Section 3.2.2 and inserts two appendices while renumbering existing ones. Publication headers and contact information change, but the main narrative and most appendix prose are retained.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn to show the generative model, temporal-gap context processing and neural-operator module in three panels. Table 25 is added. Other result figures and table structures are retained, with ordinary relocation and page reflow.

improvement.justification: Corrected loss equations, additional architecture details, explicit resource-access information and expanded research positioning improve clarity and reproducibility. The fine-tuning study adds useful preliminary evidence, although its claim of no catastrophic forgetting exceeds the limited, mixed window-count results in Table 25. With the original benchmark evidence retained, these changes support a limited net improvement.
